clinician.trajectory_summary: A 56-year-old woman with history of autoimmune hypothyroidism presented with classic features of primary adrenal insufficiency including skin hyperpigmentation, severe hyponatremia (127 mEq/L), hyperkalemia (6.3 mEq/L), hypomagnesemia (1.23 mg/dL), metabolic acidosis, and exacerbated renal failure (Cr 1.65 mg/dL), accompanied by asthenia, vomiting, and weight loss. Given recurrent vomiting and psychiatric history, an eating disorder was initially suspected, but psychiatric consultation excluded anorexia nervosa and bulimia due to absence of self-induced vomiting and atypical electrolyte patterns inconsistent with purging behaviors. Endocrinology evaluation suspected Addison's disease based on the characteristic electrolyte abnormalities and hyperpigmentation. Serologic testing confirmed positive anti-21-hydroxylase antibodies, establishing the autoimmune etiology. Treatment with dexamethasone produced dramatic clinical improvement with normalization of electrolytes (sodium 135 mEq/L, potassium 4.2 mEq/L, magnesium 1.7 mg/dL, creatinine 1.0 mg/dL) prior to discharge.
